STANDING COMMITTEE ON CONSUMER AND CORPORATE AFFAIRS AND GOVERNMENT OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which arises from an incident that took place after the meeting of the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Government Operations last Thursday, March 21, 1991.
Briefly, the member for Calgary West rose in the House last Thursday after and put before Your Honour the matter of recorded minutes without a quorum. Mr. Speaker said at that time, and I quote:
Again the hon. member for Calgary West has raised a matter which I think is properly still a matter for the committee. If his position is well founded, I am sure that some discussion with those who do our printing for us would probably keep the situation under control.
In a nutshell, Mr. Speaker, you reiterated what you have said so many times before: that a committee must resolve problems within the committee.
Last Friday afternoon, the day following the committee meeting, I was informed by an editor of committee reporting that the PMO ordered the minutes of the meeting following Mr. Spicer's appearance removed from the record. In Beauchesne's fifth edition citation 41(1) is quite clear on this matter. It states:
The control of the House over its publications is absolute.
It goes on in citation 75 as follows:
Committee reports and the verbatim transcripts of committee
hearings are documents published under the authority of the House
and are entitled to the same absolute privilege as House documents.
Interference by the Prime Minister's office in the printing of a committee proceeding is contempt of the authority of the House and its committees.
Furthermore, I submit that while this contempt arose from a committee meeting, it has nothing to do with the proceedings of the committee and everything to do with interference in the committee report by the PMO.
As a contempt, it is the Speaker who should permit a motion to be put to the floor. It is not a question for the committee to decide. Should you find that I have a basis of privilege in this matter, Mr. Speaker, I have prepared the appropriate motion and I am prepared to move it.

I rose in the House a week ago Thursday to make sure that the House was seized of the matter. It is, as you indicated at that time, Sir, a House matter. I do not know of any occasion in my time in this place where "the Prime Minister's office", whatever that is, has ordered the House to do anything or a House committee to do anything.
If one wants to make this allegation, I think one should be prepared to put one's personal reputation on the line and provide some evidence for the allegation.

Mr. Speaker, as you will recall from my interventions of last Thursday, I was definitely present at the meeting in question, and quite a meeting it was.
I just want to bring one or two items to the attention of the Chair which might assist it in deliberating on this issue.
While it is true, as Mr. Speaker has often said, that committees are masters of their own business, as indicated in Beauchesne's, it is only true provided committees follow the rules set down by this House and its Standing Orders. We know that to be the case as well.
That is why the issue the control of all publications of the House falls within the jurisdiction of the House. That extends as well to the authority of the House over the publications of committees. As far as I am concerned, a transcript of a committee is the same as Hansard. It is the Hansard of the committee, if I can put it that way.
There is a long-standing tradition in parliamentary committees of quorum being defined in two ways. There is a formal quorum for the purpose of voting. There is also what is commonly referred to as mini quorum in our parliamentary jargon. That means to say that at any time when four members are present they can hear witnesses, Hansard or the parliamentary publication of the committee is published and so on, but votes cannot be taken.
The point I am making is that notwithstanding the fact that the committee might have lost its full quorum for a period, if mini quorum were still present a publication of the proceedings was indeed not only in order, but necessary according to our tradition.
The allegation is to determine whether or not interference has taken place with the publication of the report pursuant to the mini quorum which was obviously there.
To that extent I feel that if the issue were brought to the attention of the parliamentary committee pursuant to the prima facie information brought before us today, the committee could be seized of all the details and render a recommendation to the House on the issue.
It is not up to this House at this point to bring forward the clerk of the committee to the bar or whomever else. That is the role of the parliamentary Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. What this House has to decide is whether or not there is a prima facie case of privilege. You will make that determination at some point, Mr. Speaker, and, if you deem there is a prima facie case of privilege pursuant to the allegation made by the hon. member for Nickel Belt, I would submit that the issue can and should be referred to the appropriate parliamentary committee, notwithstanding the remarks that have been made by the hon. government Whip.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising to speak on Bill C-79 and the motion that is before the House as a result of the Senate amendments.
The House is aware that at 5.58 p.m. last Thursday, the government moved to try to quickly pass Bill C-79. There was a one-minute debate by the minister introducing it and a 30-second response by the Liberal member for Kingston and the Islands. Then the government Whip moved the previous question which, basical-

ly, prevents any member of this House from introducing any amendments.
The government did that with the full knowledge that I had amendments to the legislation as it came from the Senate. I believe that the Senate has closed one loophole, but it has built a much bigger credibility gap. This move will come to haunt this House of Commons and will come to haunt the Senate if this motion is passed without amendment.
I believe that the Senate acted in good faith. It saw in the bill which originally came from the House of Commons that it is possible for a member of this House or of the Senate who was under investigation to go quickly to the Board of Internal Economy or the equivalent committee of the Senate and ask that body to give an opinion on the issue of whether or not that money, service or premise was being used for the proper purposes.
According to the Senate, that created a chance for delay. If a member went to the Board of Internal Economy at the last minute, the board may take four, five or six weeks to render an opinion. Because that opinion had to be given to a judge, a member of Parliament or a Senator could end up delaying the work of a police officer and could prevent a search warrant or some other appropriate document from being served at the appropriate time.
If that was all that a Senate amendment did, that would be an improvement to the legislation. However, the Senate went much further. It took away all obligation on the part of the board to give the opinion to the police officer who was conducting an investigation. A police officer could be aware that the board has given an opinion. The board may have given an opinion to the member that what he or she did was acceptable, but that board may also have given an opinion that what the member of Parliament or the senator did was unacceptable under our rules and under the by-laws that the board will be introducing.
If the board in its wisdom decided that it was not going to issue that opinion to a police officer, we would all live under a cloud of doubt because that police officer in going forward to get a search warrant or something else should, and probably would, indicate that he sought an
opinion that was available from the Board of Internal Economy, that the Board of Internal Economy had made that decision but refuses to give it to the police officer.
By making the whole issue of whether or not the board gives its opinion to a police officer discretionary, we put ourselves under a real cloud of doubt. I can bet that if the board refuses to give an opinion on the actions of a certain member, you can be assured that the media and the public will assume that the board is covering up for that member. They will automatically assume that the board's opinion was unfavourable to that member.
We are being asked by the quick actions of this government to vote now on a measure that is only going to cause unnecessary havoc and concern for members of this House in the future. I believe that if an opinion has already been made by the board-we are not talking about delay- then that opinion should be given forthwith to the police officers doing the investigation.
If the board has not made a decision, or given an opinion, then there should be no obligation on the part of anyone to act because then we could be perceived as delaying. But if the opinion is already made by this board or by its equivalent in the Senate, then that should be given to a police officer and that information can be used by the officer as he or she sees fit.
We are not talking about delay. We are talking about making sure that there is no perception whatsoever that the Board of Internal Economy is covering up any possible criminal wrongdoing by a member of this House or that the Senate is doing the equivalent thing with one of its members.
In answer to some questions I asked about this issue on Friday, the government said that all members can be rest assured that nothing devious is going to happen because all parties are represented on the Board of Internal Economy. That is true for this House, but it is also true that as a result of Bill C-79 members of the board are going to have to sign an oath of secrecy. We will not know what happened at a board meeting, whether the government majority on the board used its majority to prevent a ruling from being released to the police. We will never know what has happened.
We cannot be guaranteed that the board will act in the best interests of all members of this House. As I said, every time the board decides not to give an opinion, the
March 26, 1991

public will assume that the member is guilty of some breach.
We have a problem with what we are being asked to vote on today. We have a problem with perception. We have a problem with fairness. That problem becomes even worse when you think about the Senate because at least on the Board of Internal Economy of the House all three parties are represented. In the Senate it is just the Liberals and the Conservatives, people who are unelected, people who never have to face the scrutiny of the public. We saw how cavalier they can be in their treatment of the public purse with their request for $153 a day attendance bonus. Last week we heard the Speaker rule that the method they used to try and guarantee themselves this bonus went against the laws of this land and the rules of the House.
We would have a situation where a committee of the Senate, meeting in secret, could decide that it does not want to issue opinions to police officers and there is nothing that can be done about it.
What we have offered, and I have given copies to the other parties, is a couple of amendments. I will read one of them:
For greater certainty, if an opinion has been given by the Board in relation to the use by a member of funds, goods, services and premises referred to in subsection 52.6(1), the Board shall provide the opinion to the peace officer forthwith.
That is a reasonable amendment. I have a companion amendment to that to make sure that the law is covered in both clauses and both areas this is referring to. We are not talking about delay. We are saying that only if an opinion has been given by the board already, then it must be given to the police officer forthwith. It is not up to the majority on the board. It is not up to the Senate secret committee to make that decision. The board should be able to live with the opinions it has made and it should make those opinions public.
Unfortunately, the manoeuvring that took place at 5.58 p.m. on Thursday prevented the New Democratic Party from making those amendments in the House. The government is preventing debate on this very important matter. The Liberal Party, through its spokesman, allowed that to happen. We are in a situation now where we are dealing with flawed legislation.
Government Orders
We are dealing with something which will be a time bomb, ticking away, waiting for some member in the future, some senator in the future to be charged.
The whole reason for setting up the committee to review the Parliament of Canada Act was to make sure that we had procedures in place that protected members, but also did not put them above the law, that did not make us above the law, but at the same time, people would understand what the rules of the game are and that we have procedures in place. That is why we are calling for bylaws to be made by the Board of Internal Economy. That is why we are calling for a process where there is an investigation of a member. All of that was to make sure that we got out of the problems we faced in the past.
Now, by a last minute amendment coming from the Senate, and by the manoeuvrings that took place in this House on Thursday evening, we are facing a situation which is taking us full circle, back to where we started a year and a half ago when this committee first started to work.
There have been suggestions by others that there are other ways out of this mess. It has been suggested to me in private that perhaps what the Board of Internal Economy should do as its first order of business is to pass a bylaw that would make all of its opinions public in the case of a police officer's investigation. That is a possible way out.
I have to raise the question: Do we have the same guarantees that the Senate committee would do the same thing? They have no sense of public responsibility. There is no way of dealing with senators who act in arrogance. There is no way of dealing with senators who choose to continue to act in secret.
As members of the House, our obligation is to try and pass the best legislation possible. I think it is important that we have these amendments before this House. If we do not have these amendments before this House, we have no guarantee that members will be treated equally in the future. We have no guarantee that the board will make the wisest decision. A police officer making an investigation has no guarantee that he or she will have access to a board opinion that is ready. A judge has no guarantee that he or she will be given access to that board opinion, all of this because the government wants to act in haste.

March 26, 1991
Government Orders
The Parliament of Canada Act committee has basically been non-partisan. It has basically tried to resolve its issues. On Thursday of last week the government moved with undue haste. It knew that these amendments were coming. I had informed the government earlier that day that these amendments would be in front of the legislative clerk. It was that same day that the actual wording for the amendment that I read earlier and its companion amendment were produced.
Had the government waited a few hours, had they consulted, the government and the Official Opposition would have known the wording. There was no talk of delay. There was no talk of stalling. We had a legitimate concern with this legislation. We still have that legitimate concern.
Unfortunately as a result of the motion by the government Whip, "That this question be now put", those amendments which would protect members, which would protect the reputation of this House cannot be put before this very House.
I would ask, Mr. Speaker, that you seek unanimous consent of this House that the amendments that I referred to be allowed to be placed on the Order Paper. I would make that a motion at this time.

Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, I think that states the problem. Here we are in a situation where the Liberal opposition and the government have the amendments. We have a situation where amendments that would clear the reputation of this House-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order please. I do not understand why the hon. member speaks before the House. In presenting his motion, his time is over.
Questions and comments, the hon. member for Victoria.

Mr. Speaker, my comment first of all, I guess to set up the question, arises out of my
absolute astonishment that this issue has arisen. There are many duties we have as members of Parliament. It is not possible always for us to follow in detail the intricacies of each bill. It is our responsibility, which we fulfil, to read the legislation and to consider it before we vote.
I had frankly understood that this issue and the issue of Bill C-79 had been settled some time ago. I guess when things head off to the other place we have a sense of it disappearing, usually off into the ether, some time to return without any change.
Here we have a case where the Senate has acted and in which it appears both the Liberals and the Conservatives, who not only dominate the Senate, but there really are no members other than a couple of independents who do not have a Liberal or a Conservative background, essentially six my friend indicates. Essentially it is a Conservative and Liberal institution. That institution sometimes gets public attention, as it did last fall, but here again it interferes with the legislative process and does so for what would appear to me on the face of it to be highly partisan reasons. The Senate amends this legislation which was designed to protect the public interest, and Parliament as well, the public interest in having an independent Parliament along with the public interest that wrongdoing be properly prosecuted; that that very delicate bill, which did provide that balance, has now been altered by the Liberals and Conservatives in the Senate. The bill comes back to this House, and what happens? The Liberals and Conservatives in this House gang up to endorse and rubber-stamp this interference in the will of this House on this bill.
Frankly, it leaves me absolutely mystified. I would like to ask the member for Churchill, who has spoken already so eloquently on this, if he could speculate for us why the Liberals and Conservatives are taking this position. He has been able to participate more carefully than I in some of the discussions and in following the details of this bill. Why would the Liberals and Conservatives want to do this? Why would it not be an absolutely obvious thing that the report to the Board of Internal Economy, or to the committee, would be made available to the peace officer and to the judge?
It seems to me so absolutely obvious, if the interests of justice are to be maintained. How come the Liberals and Conservatives not only have allowed this to happen, but
March 26, 1991

don't appear to be interested in participating in this debate?

The member for Victoria asked me to speculate, to use my imagination. I do not think I have enough time to deal with all the possible scenarios.
But, let me say this, even assuming that there is no attempt at a cover-up, and even assuming that this wasn't just an accident, the problem is that it is much more comfortable for a committee in the Senate, or for the Board of Internal Economy, to make its decisions behind closed doors and not to be accountable to anyone.
People can be very comfortable with that way of doing things. But when there is a police investigation and when a police officer comes to the Board of Internal Economy, and when the police officer knows that the board has made a decision or that the equivalent committee in the Senate has made a decision-that decision is already made, there is no possibility of us delaying anything, or the board or the House being perceived as delaying anything-then I believe that the board has a public responsibility to provide that information.
If it means that the board has to be more careful when it makes a decision, if it means it has to keep clear and accurate records of its proceedings, well, Mr. Speaker, I cannot think of a more appropriate place than for the House of Commons and its committees to keep accurate records.
I believe that if the board has looked at a member's budget and how that member has spent his budget, and it believes that that was not done under the rules of this House, then there should be no question, there should be no discretion, the board should have an obligation to give that information to a police officer and then it is up to the judge and jury to make a decision on the broader aspects of wrongdoing.
If we have a rule in this House that says you cannot spend money in such a way that it comes back to your own pocket, or to your spouse's pocket-and that is indeed happening-then I think the board has to say that that is not acceptable. I think the board has that obligation.
With regard to the question, it may well be that some people are comfortable with the old way of doing things,
Government Orders
and maybe some people think the board should not have to be that careful when it makes its opinions. But I think the board does have that obligation.
I have clearly put our amendments in such a way that we can never be charged with delaying the due process of a police investigation.
I have not said that the board must have the right to give an opinion before the police officer can go any further. I have said that the board only acts where the information is ready and where it can present it to a police officer. I am saying that where the information is ready it is not discretionary; it must be given to the police officer. We cannot be perceived in any way, shape or form of being engaged in a cover-up of our own members.

Mr. Speaker, I too have a question for the hon. member.
As the House knows, the other day the government introduced a package of so-called reforms to the Standing Orders, ostensibly to bring democracy back to the House of Commons and that people would perceive democracy to be existing in the House of Commons. In actual fact those of us who understand the orders that govern this House know that the very opposite is the case. It would in fact turn the government party in this House into nothing less than a dictatorship.
I just want to ask the hon. member whether or not the example we have just seen in the House today which arose from procedural manoeuvring in the House by both the government and the Official Opposition over the last couple of weeks is the kind of activity that will ultimately destroy democracy in this House.

Mr. Speaker, I think the member for Beaches-Woodbine has managed to raise some of the other issues that are before the public.
If through procedural gains the government, with the compliance of the Official Opposition, has prevented amendments from coming forward on this very important matter, where we are talking about police investigations of members of this House or members of the Senate, where we see the rules being used to prevent a debate over what are the obligations of the Board of Internal Economy when there is a police investigation,

March 26, 1991
Government Orders
we have to be worried about the over-all agenda and the government's way of doing things.
I may have problems with the rule changes, but we are not debating them at the present time. What I am afraid of-and I think the member who asked the question is aware of it-is that we already had this abuse of the rules. If anything, the rule changes that are coming down perhaps later today or tomorrow in this House make it that much more difficult for myself or some other member who is in opposition to the government or some public group that wants to appear before a legislative committee of this House. Those rules are designed in such a way as to make it more difficult for an opposition member or a government backbencher, as somebody pointed out. For that matter, under the proposed rules legislative committees would not even hear from public groups that oppose government's legislation. That is taken away.
What happened last Thursday at two minutes to six o'clock is unfortunately an indication of where this government goes with all rule changes.

Mr. Speaker, I was looking across the aisle at my hon. friend from Peace River who I suspect was going to make some comments on the important issue raised by my hon. friend from Churchill.
I must say it is with a heavy heart today that we have to be here taking up time when we should be talking about agriculture. As far as I am concerned, farming is the backbone of much of our economy. The farmers are struggling. There is a whole set of issues that ought to be addressed immediately with almost a sense of crisis in some sectors of the agricultural community. We would like to do so but we can only do what the government asks us to do, as you well know, Mr. Speaker, that is to talk about a rather peculiar turn of events regarding Bill C-79.
Before I talk about Bill C-79, I want to say that I can only assume that the government is trying to put a fast one over on the people of Canada. After all, I remember last Thursday. I have just to take a moment to explain last Thursday because it is so germane to the debate today.
Last Thursday we were debating agriculture. It was appropriate. It was a good discussion. There were some
excellent debates. As a matter of fact they were some of the most enlightened debates I have heard in this House in a long time. They showed a real concern about agriculture and a want to get on with dealing with these issues.
We had agreed that we would complete report stage of Bill C-98.1 left some direction with my hon. colleagues which said "just prior to six o'clock let's wrap up this stage of the deliberations so that the report stage can pass and we can get on with debating agriculture", we thought today. Unfortunately it looks like that is not the case. In other words, we were trying to facilitate the business of the House by wrapping up by six o'clock so that the appropriate votes could take place. In other words, it was in good faith, above the table, honest, and positive. We were trying to do the best job we could as a positive and effective opposition.
Then, out of the blue we get a left hook coming at us.
A right hook.

First of all it was a right hook where the government stood up in a split second and said: "Aha, maybe we can put a fast one over on the opposition", namely the New Democrats. It stood up and introduced Bill C-79 out of the blue. There were no discussions. There had been no consultation. It was out of the absolute blue.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I may remind the hon. member that a question of privilege was raised by the hon. member for Churchill, that the Speaker has already ruled on the incident described by the hon. member, and that the Standing Orders of the House were applied. I would therefore ask the hon. member for Kamloops to be prudent in his comments.

Mr. Speaker, the government may have technically been following the rules, but it tried to sneak one past us. It tried at the last minute, just seconds before the House would normally rise for the day, to introduce a piece of legislation when no one was watching. No one was watching. I am not concerned about us here. There were some opposition members here, but what about the people of Canada? That is who the government was trying to pull a fast one on, not us. We are on top of this.
March 26, 1991

This is my disappointing comment. My friends in the Liberal Party co-operated with the government. My hon. friend for Kingston and the Islands stood in his place. He usually speaks for 20 minutes. Normally he has a lot of intelligent things to say. He has a contribution to make to debate, so when he stands we always assume we are going to have a full deliberation.
He spoke for only 20 seconds. This was the first time in his life my hon. friend for Kingston and the Islands has ever spoken for 20 seconds. Why? It was to allow the government, as my hon. friend from Churchill has explained, to pass another sneaky motion which would eliminate any possibility of this motion being amended.
We support the bill.

That is the point that I am trying to make. My hon. colleague from Kingston and the Islands yells out that they support the government, that they support this. We do not.
We think that there is something very seriously flawed with this particular legislation. My hon. friend from Prince George-Peace River is rattling his head. I can hear him from here, right across the entire aisle.
I know my hon. friends on the government benches find the opposition obstructive. They do not want to have debate in the House of Commons. They do not want to have a reaction to the government's Draconian legislation. They want to slip fast ones through to manipulate the House. I will tell you, Mr. Speaker: the people of Canada are fed up with this government manipulating the House of Commons on behalf of the people of Canada.
Let me get back to the business at hand. I am a member of the Board of Internal Economy. I am proud to be a member of that board. A lot of people in Canada wonder what it is this board does. There has been a veil of questions around this particular board. People ask me what it is we do. I explain what we do and so on. There is an element of jitteriness. We appreciate that we need a group to manage the affairs of the parliamentary precincts and people on that board, in my judgment, work very hard and are very dedicated to the task.
However, there is an element of some question. I put it at that, nothing more than that.
Government Orders
Then the government introduced Bill C-79, and again there was another element of question and concern. What kind of powers are we giving this board? Most of what goes on in there is not in the public purview. Then we see in the legislation-and I supported this legislation up until very recently, with the exception of the point raised by my hon. friend from Churchill-where it says that every member of the board, as soon as practicable after becoming a member of the board, shall take before the Clerk of the House of Commons an oath of affirmation, fidelity and secrecy.
As soon as we start operating in secret, people become somewhat suspicious, for good reason. The one thing we know as parliamentarians is that we want to be up-front. We want to have things on the table. We want to be in the open. After all, we are servants of the people. Whenever we start to agree to do things in secret, people begin to wonder.
Form 3, which all of us on the Board of Internal Economy will sign, says "I"-and you fill in your name-"do solemnly swear or affirm that I will faithfully, truly, and to the best of my judgment, skill and ability execute and perform the duties required of me as a member of the Board of Internal Economy of the House of Commons, so help me God". It goes on: "I further solemnly swear or affirm that I will not communicate or allow to be communicated to any person without due authority in that behalf any information related to matters of employment and staff relations, tenders, security, investigations in relation to a member of the House of Commons".
In other words, as a member of the board, I will swear an oath that I will not communicate, ever, any investigations in relation to a member of the House of Commons.
That is because it would not be right if you did communicate it.

I hear an echo. The point is right. To communicate in matters of this perhaps would be highly questionable. However, that is what we agree to do.
What are we saying, then? Let us make sure that we have taken every precaution to ensure that whatever decision that board makes is not only right in terms of the law but is perceived to be right in terms of the law.

March 26, 1991
Government Orders
The hon. member for Churchill has worked on Bill C-79 from the outset, file has spent literally hundreds of hours examining, analysing, discussing, and in thoughtful introspection in terms of the implication of this legislation. I mean that with all sincerity. He has identified a small flaw in the legislation that came back from the Senate.
He offers the following clarification so the people of Canada will know full well that if a member of Parliament is being investigated by the RCMP there will be no cover-up. There was a concern in the past that there were cover-ups, that the Board of Internal Economy and other investigations were being influenced in terms of being able to allow the RCMP to carry out its investigations effectively.
Again, not only must we be doing the right thing. We must be perceived to be doing the right thing.
The hon. member for Churchill has picked up on a problem with the amendment returned from the Senate. He has suggested:
That Bill C-79 be amended by adding after line 18 on page 8 the
following:
"52.7(1.1) For greater certainty, if an opinion has been given by the Board in relation to the use by a member of funds, goods, services and premises referred to in subsection 52.6(1), the Board shall provide the opinion to the peace officer forthwith".
Then he suggested:
That amendment 6 be amended to read as follows:
"Strike out lines 19 to 29, page 8, clause (2) and substitute the
following:
(2) Where an opinion is provided to a peace officer to subsection (1) or the peace officer has been advised by the Board that an application under subsection 52.6(2) has been made by the member of the House of Commons to whom the investigation relates and the Committee has given an opinion and where an application for a process is made to a judge, the judge shall consider it in determining whether to issue the process."
It is perfectly clear, absolutely clear. It is a straightforward and simple amendment that would rectify any concern about the whole process so that Canadian citizens could feel secure and comforted to know that a fair evaluation will take place by the Board of Internal Economy and that the information will be passed along to the most appropriate persons.
That is perfectly clear, perfectly obvious. It is the right thing to do. Yet the government has, in its mysterious way, taken steps to ensure that this will not take place, that this change will not occur.
Let us set aside the House of Commons because we have a good check and balance system. All members of the House, all recognized parties of the House, are at least represented on the Board of Internal Economy.
In the Senate and its committee, with a similar operation, such is not the case. First of all, we are dealing with people who are not elected by the people of Canada. They have been appointed for a variety of reasons, because they are hacks, flacks, or bagmen, or for some other reason, by the Prime Minister of the day to the Upper House. Only two political parties sit there.
I personally do not have that much faith in the integrity of the Senate of Canada after seeing its decision to try to slip something through the back door. You referred to the thoughtful comments and the decision of the Speaker on a previous occasion, Mr. Speaker. You will only appreciate too well that the Speaker felt it was his job to point out the inappropriateness of the Senate using the back-door routine to try to get themselves a raise.
In other words, if you want to pay yourself $153 a day to show up for work then do it up-front, do it through the appropriate process. They tried a rather devious route and thank goodness the Speaker stood up, pointed that out and said it was inappropriate and unacceptable in a democratic system.
Something similar may be happening here. There is a back-door routine and the government is not permitting what anybody would consider to be a fair, just, or equitable resolution to the particular problem that has been pointed out in the motion coming back from the Upper House.
Not only are we concerned about the process. Why is it that there has been this duplicity between the Liberals and the Conservatives to try to fast-track this piece of legislation so that the New Democrats will not have a chance to clarify the legislation through amendment? Why would they do that?
I do not know. It is that kind of duplicity, that kind of working together to protect one another, which causes us concerns in this party regarding the Senate. Essentially
March 26, 1991

Government Orders
there are only those two parties represented in the Senate. There are some Independents, but basically there are those two parties.
I do not want to start mentioning names. I do not think that would be appropriate. However, we have some pretty cosy arrangements being provided and some secret examinations going on in terms of some of their members' conduct. I do not think the people of Canada have faith in that system. That is why we are saying that it needs to be clarified. Nothing more, just clarified, so that everybody understands what the process is, everybody buys into the process and says: "Yes, this is a decent process. This is a good process. This is an up-front process. This is a just, fair, equitable process".
Why is the government against that? Why would it be against considering something that is so obviously positive and so obviously good?
We have received all sorts of advice from procedural experts. We have received all sorts of suggestions from people who watch this very closely. They say that what the hon. member for Churchill is proposing is probably soft, if anything, but at least it is a move in the right direction. I hate to say this because I have many friends with the caucus opposite and in the Liberal Party, but they have refused to accept this. We can only say that this is a very serious situation.
Tied in with this is the whole matter of changing the way this House of Commons operates, the Standing Orders, and tossing a hundred-plus years of regulation, rule, and tradition out the window to enable the government to implement with minimal opposition, minimal fuss, its oppressive agenda on the people of Canada.
Obviously we will not stand for that, and we are not going to stand for this. We are just not going to turn a blind eye and let these organizations that already work in secret have the legislative authority to make decisions regarding the conduct of members of Parliament or senators regarding police investigations and hold that under some kind of cloud. That is not the way to proceed. I want to speak very positively in support of these two amendments. I think that my hon. friend from Churchill did the right thing when he asked for unanimous consent for the government to now reconsider its silliness and permit consideration of these two amendments.
I would like to think that before we end this debate, we will again make that suggestion. Perhaps it would be appropriate to hear from other members. Many members here have a lot to say about this issue. If necessary, we are prepared to speak all day and all day tomorrow and beyond on this because we just do not feel comfortable at all. As a matter of fact, we would not even consider supporting legislation that is so obviously flawed when my hon. colleague from Churchill has provided a simple amendment which would rectify the situation.
We will continue to discuss and debate this in hopes that eventually the government will see the wisdom of following our advice.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the New Democratic Party House leader, as a member of the committee, would enlighten us as to why we are faced with this unique opposition only by the New Democratic Party. Where is the voice of the Official Opposition, the Liberal Party of Canada?
In the member's opinion, is it a presumption that it may be in government and that it would like this kind of protection when it is in government? Surely, as a new member, I would would like to be disabused of that concept. If, indeed, that is his opinion, then the Canadian public should hear it. Why is the Liberal Party so silent on this issue today? Why is it, in its years of experience, just as the Tories have been governing, when there have been errant members, that the cops should be allowed to go directly into this without any political interference? Cops are not interfered with by ordinary citizens. Why should they be interfered with by politicians?
I want to ask my good friend the House leader of the New Democratic Party to enlighten me, as a novice to this place and to this whole system of politics, why would the Liberal Party be opposed to our amendments?
Please do not disappoint me. Do not tell me the Liberal Party is cynical. I am ready for anything.

Mr. Speaker, this is a most serious question raised by my hon. colleague. I suspect, just by looking at the faces of all members interested in this issue, that it is a question on the minds of a lot of people. Why are the Liberals involved in what appears to be a very draconian

March 26, 1991
Government Orders
and sinister move to cover up and to establish, in a sense, almost two levels of justice?
Right.
One for the people of Canada and a separate one for-
For members under investigation.

Well, members under investigation, but members of Parliament and Senators.
I think I speak for everyone in the New Democratic Party caucus when I say that we feel there should be one justice system.
Hear, hear.

We can only accept one justice system.
My hon. friend, the government Whip is in his place listening carefully and we look forward to his remarks. I think perhaps, he has a different interpretation of the seriousness of this problem.
We might argue the technicalities and he might feel that in terms of the exact letter of the law, particularly as it applies to subsection 52.7 and 52.6, that technically we are overly concerned. Is it not appropriate that there be no question whatsoever? My hon. friend from Churchill raised this critical question and we might debate how critical it is.
From the fact that it has been raised and no one in the Liberal or Conservative parties have even discussed or argued against it, we can only assume that they are feeling very uncomfortable today.
Shame, shame.

They are feeling a part of a process that is going to get us as members of Parliament in big trouble if we give the impression that there are two justice systems. I appeal to my friends across the aisle in the Conservative Party and my colleagues in the Liberal Party to participate in this debate. Then I can determine from their points of view if my friend from Churchill has misinterpreted this amendment. I do not think he has. There is a serious problem of perception, and it is imperative that collectively all of us say that there is one justice system, one for members of Parliament and the people of Canada, and no special treatment for anybody in this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to hear all the applause from the NDP benches. I must say that the hon. member for Kamloops surprises me; he is trying to allege there is some kind of sinister plot going on here, if I can quote his words. This particular bill, Bill C-79, was introduced in this House in June of last year and I well recall that the House leader of the New Democratic Party wanted to put this bill through all stages in one day. It was only the objections of our party which saved this bill from being passed at that time-
Order.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. On a point of order, the hon. member for Churchill.

Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member is referring to June of last year, he will find that it was the New Democratic Party that refused to allow it to go through in all stages. We said there were some flaws; we insisted that it be sent to committee.

Obviously that was not a point of order, and I maintain the position that it was our party that objected to having that bill passed at all stages in its original form in June 1990.
We then had the outraged statements of the member for Kamloops. He said this bill was a travesty and was now opposed to it, because he had seen the good reasons we put forward for opposition to the bill in its original form. The bill was referred to a special committee.
I believe the hon. member for Churchill was a member of that special committee. I think he sat on it throughout the summer. The government Whip says it was only half the time but nevertheless I understand he appeared at the committee and took part in its deliberations. The committee reported to this House in November 1990 and recommended some very worth-while changes to the bill. Those changes were agreed upon and the bill was passed on November 30 in this House.
Now the bill has come back from the Senate with a couple of amendments which are technical in nature which we in our party support. I stood up the other day when the Senate amendments were moved for second reading and indicated my support and the support of our party for those amendments. We stand by that support.

Hear, hear.
March 26, 1991

I didn't hear anything in what the hon. member for Kamloops said that indicated that support was withdrawn by his party. He supports those amendments also.
What I understand is that the member for Churchill has had a death-bed repentance of some kind and thinks he has to make more amendments because he somehow feels left out.
I say to the hon. member for Kamloops, who supported this bill on his own admission until the other day, that he should be standing up praising the government and allowing this bill to go through. Everyone agrees with it. The only person who has a problem is the hon. member for Churchill, and we all saw how he behaved the other day when he found that he was not going to be able to move his amendments.
Furthermore, I suggest that the hon. member for Kamloops knows full well that it would be out of order for the hon. member for Churchill to move amendments to this bill at this stage. The bill has been amended and passed in this House. The Senate amendments only are before us; we cannot provide other amendments at this stage to this bill. The hon. member for Kamloops knows that and I suggest he stand up right now and admit it. This whole thing is a facade and a fraud that he is trying to put over on this House and convince the Canadian people that somehow there is some kind of cover-up going on here, which there is not.

Mr. Speaker, methinks my hon. friend protesteth too much. He gets a little excited. We must have touched a bit of a nerve when we suggested that.
Let me explain what actually happened, because obviously my hon. friend was missing during part of the deliberations.
We are not debating a bill, we are debating a motion. My hon. friend should know that. Consequently when he said that we supported Bill C-79, we are not talking about Bill C-79 today.
We are talking about a motion referring to Bill C-79 today. He knows better than that, but is obviously trying to cover some tracks that are pretty murky at the moment.
While we supported Bill C-79-

Before it was amended.
Government Orders

Before it was amended by your friends in the Senate, yes, we supported Bill C-79. It was then altered and we do not support the alteration. From the day it came back from the Senate, my hon. colleague for Churchill, who was the representative of the New Democratic Party during consideration of Bill C-79, indicated clearly to my hon. friend the government Whip, the Government House Leader, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Government House Leader and, presumably, similar counterparts in the Liberal Party that we had serious concerns and we were going to suggest we amend the motion.
My hon. friend then went to the law clerks who were drafting the motion. We communicated that to not only the Parliamentary Secretary of the Government House Leader, but the Deputy House Leader as well. He was waiting to hear back from the clerks in conclusion.
Our track record on this is perfectly clean, perfectly clear and perfectly straightforward. I have yet to hear from my hon. friends why they are supporting-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate. The hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is time someone put on the record the events connected with the motion before us which, in the Senate, led to a number of comments by senators which I feel are justified and to amendments that reflect an entity that is different from our own.
To be perfectly clear, the amendments before us today, which are being proposed by the Senate, deal with a situation that somewhat differs from ours in that the Senate's board of internal economy is not organized the same way. The Speaker of the House of Commons is both member and Chairman of the Board of Internal Economy of the House of Commons. That is not the case in the Senate. The Speaker of the Senate does not automatically chair the Senate's committee on internal economy which is, in fact, a Standing Committee of the Senate that regularly reports to the Senate. So the procedure differs somewhat from what is customary here in the House of Commons.
Second, the amendments confirm these differences and provide for intersessional authority. The point is, that when Parliament is prorogued, since the Senate's internal economy committee is a Standing Committee, it

March 26, 1991
Government Orders
would immediately lose its powers and be unable to pursue any further activities. The Senate therefore proposes an amendment that would provide for intersessional authority, so that senators would be able to continue to work during a period of prorogation of Parliament.
In fact, during the debate in the Senate, there was some discussion on section 52.7.

I will use my second language so that members of the House will understand there was no plot and no cover up. There was absolutely nothing done to tiy and change the spirit and the objectives that we had all tried to reach in getting Bill C-79 before Parliament.
I think it is a first in terms of parliamentary democracy that we now have a bill that guarantees in the House of Commons full representation to all parties on the Board of Internal Economy. One only has to look back some years ago when the government was in total command of that committee.
Today all parties have a representative on the Board of Internal Economy and that assures some justice and some equity in matters dealing with all parties and all members.
In my view there is no other way of assuring a non-partisan approach to the issues we deal with on the Board of Internal Economy, of which I am a member, and so is the member for Kamloops, who is the representative of his party.
The question arose in debate in the Senate as to our intent, our motive, our purpose. It was to give members of this House and of the Senate an opportunity to have an adjudication by their peers, by the Board of Internal Economy, of the expenditure of public funds entrusted to them to administer their offices and other things. We also wanted to put in place a system which would allow us, members of Parliament, to ask the board for an interpretation, an opinion as to the expenditures of funds in the operations of our constituency and House of Commons offices.
I see nothing wrong with that. I see absolutely nothing wrong with that. I think it is a step in the right direction.
If a member is concerned or has doubt about what he is about to do in terms of expenditure or what he is about to do in terms of administering his office, then he can go to the board and ask for its opinion. He can say to the board: "What do you think of this proposal", and the board will answer either that it is okay or: "No, we do not agree, therefore you cannot do it".
The question that arose in the Senate and arose in my mind, because when we passed the bill at third reading an amendment was passed about which I had some hesitation, but nevertheless with the assurance of all parties, I thought I will not pursue that. I will not pursue it because maybe the Senate will agree that there could be here a review of that clause, which is clause 52.7.
Clause 52.7(2) read this way: "Where an opinion is provided to a peace officer, pursuant to subsection (1)", and the text went on to say, "or", and I underline "or", "the peace officer has been advised by the board that an application under subsection 52.6(2) has been made by the member of the House of Commons to whom the investigation relates and where an application for a process is made to a judge, the judge shall be provided with the opinion and shall consider it in determining whether to issue the process".
The difficulty that I had and that some other members of this group had, was with the "or the peace officer having been advised by the board that an application under subsection 52.6". I am not a lawyer, but I am told that members of Parliament and senators sometimes get wind that an investigation is ongoing on matters pertaining to the administration of their funds, that is the funds given to them to administer their office. They get wind of this.
The possibility which I objected to, and I am thinking here in terms of an all-party position, the difficulty of that position was that if a member heard or got wind of an investigation on his administration of public funds, he could immediately ask the board for an opinion. In my judgment and the judgment of many others in the Senate, that would have stopped the process there and then. That would have prevented due process because that would have prevented the completion in my view and in the view of others of that investigation by the police officer.
March 26, 1991

It said here: "Where an opinion is provided to a peace officer pursuant to subsection (1) or the peace officer has been advised".
What if the peace officer had asked the board if it was about to give an opinion on the administration of funds from Mr. or Mrs. So-and-so? If the board said: "Yes, we are about to render that opinion," I contend that is quite logical.
There is nothing here of cover-up. It is strictly a question of interpretation. I am not a lawyer, but I do think as a legislator that a possibility could exist that the board would have been obligated to give that opinion.
If the opinion took time, it could slow the process and retard the ongoing investigation. In fact, it could stop that whole investigation. That is what we objected to, that is mainly the issue at hand here and that is why in the Senate-I can quote from the Debates extensively- that is what the argument was.
I could quote from the text of Senator MacEachen, for example: "However, if the process of going to a judge to have a search warrant or to lay a charge is linked to the work of the peace officer in laying a charge, that process cannot be completed until the opinion of the board is given. Then there is an anomaly."
At the very least, that provision was looked at and improved in my humble opinion. The purpose of the amendment in the motion before the House today is to eliminate the possibility that an opinion, having been asked, would prevent the ongoing process, that is, the legal process, to continue.
That is now eliminated. Therefore, it cannot be read to have any other interpretation.
I say to the member for Churchill-I am not quarrelling with him on the intent of his amendments-that I would agree with the purpose and the intent of his amendment. However, I say with all due respect that there is a provision in this bill that allows the House of Commons at this time to adopt this bill and look after the preoccupations of my friends from Churchill and Kamloops.
Government Orders
What we could do is to look at the section dealing with the bylaws of the board. I want to read the bylaws of the board:
Subject to section 20.7, the board may make bylaws:
(a)	respecting the calling of meetings of the board to conduct the business of the meetings;
(b)	governing the use by senators or members of Parliament of funds, goods, services and premises made available to them for the carrying out of their parliamentary functions;
(c)	prescribing the terms and conditions of the management of and accounting of funds referred to in paragraph (b);
(d)	respecting all such things that are necessary or incidental to the exercise of its powers under this section and sections 20.3 and 20.6.
We have a provision in this bill that would allow the Board of Internal Economy to pass bylaws doing exactly what the member for Churchill is proposing to the board and that would satisfy most of us. I would recommend to this House that we immediately pass this motion so we can go on to other things.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the former House leader, former Whip and very active committee member for his intervention. In particular, I want to thank him for the way he ended that intervention.
I want to point out to the House that the member for Churchill and the House leader of the New Democratic Party are just as aware as the member who has just spoken of what is in Bill C-79 and what was not touched by the Senate.
I would go one step further and read another section:
The Speaker shall table before the House of Commons the bylaws
made under this section on any of the first 30 days after the making
thereof.
If the member for Churchill really cares about this institution or the people in it, does he really want to hand the Senate the power to change what it is that he proposes? Or, does he trust the House of Commons, at least, and his member on it-the House leader of the New Democratic Party-to pass a bylaw to accomplish what it is that he sees as an oversight of the bill?
Does he really want to reject the Senate message because we made a mistake? He did, I did, the member who spoke did. The Chamber did. We passed a clause with an unseen possibility in it, which the Senate spotted. I want to pay a compliment to the Senate, as the Chamber of sober second thought, on that particular

March 26, 1991
Government Orders
clause it spotted a flaw and simply corrected it. I say thank you to the Senate. The Senate changed from a board to go back to its committee and that is a mistake. I think the Senate will be back to this Chamber some day in the next two or three years asking for a board, because I think it has created for itself an administrative structure that is unwieldy and makes it very difficult to activate the responsibilities inherent in this bill.
This bill came about and was examined by all sides of this Chamber for a purpose. We are not today, without the passage of this bill, treated like ordinary Canadians when it comes to the justice system. The securing of information from this Chamber about the behaviour of members and their utilization of the budget today, without this piece of legislation, requires a judicial process, usually a search warrant, before any information can be obtained. The Speaker has to grant permission for the warrant to be executed.
I think it is fair to say that we found that situation intolerable, that the public nature of search warrants and the fact that they are full of allegations and not proof, created difficulties for members, and in particular, members' families.
This piece of legislation is an obligation on the part of the board to provide the police and courts with information that they cannot get today. It is additional information. It is saying to the police and the courts, we will give you accurate information if you would simply come and ask.
If there is an allegation out there about the behaviour of a member, it can be dealt with quickly and expeditiously. If there is truth, or some element of truth to the allegation, it will go through an investigation and a process; If it is simply an allegation without a foundation in truth, that can be discovered and all members, all sides of the Chamber can avoid the public nature of allegations. Allegations do enormous damage. This day started at 11 a.m. with an NDP allegation about an unnamed person in the Prime Minister's office. That tars all of the members of the Prime Minister's office with a brush. It is not fair. It is simply not fair.
I would like to indicate to the colleague who spoke ahead of me, that both as board members and certainly on behalf of all the board members of my party, we would be quite willing to pass a bylaw that would require the board to give to the police officers or to the courts an opinion which is relevant to the case.
It says in the bill itself, under the bylaw section, the board of governors must make bylaws respecting all such things as are necessary or incidental to the exercise of its powers and carrying out of its functions.
Those early bylaws must deal with the way the board itself intends them to function. It can deal with the issues that are contained in these two amendments, without turning over the control to the Senate.
Abolish the Senate, says the former premier of the province of British Columbia. I did not see his legislature when he was in charge pass a motion to that effect, to abolish the Senate. It is awfully easy to sit on the side lines and snipe, but when you have the responsibility of governing, surely you have to act responsibly.
I suggest to this House there really needs to be no more time on this particular piece of legislation, that we should move to the agriculture bill. If we want more time on the agriculture bill or more time on this, I would move:
That the House continue to sit beyond the ordinary hour of daily
adjournment for the purpose of continuing consideration of the
second reading of government Bill C-79, an act to amend the
Parliament of Canada Act.
If we do not need it then we can adjourn at one o'clock or we could actually agree to consider the agricultural bill after one o'clock. At this point, I simply would ask you to put that motion.

Mr. Speaker, the motions that I was not allowed to make to this House have been the subject of debate for the last half hour and have been the subject of a number of offers and counter-offers across the floor. Considering the manoeuvring that took place at two minutes to six last Thursday, I am certainly not going to allow the same manoeuvring to take place at two minutes to one.
Our House leader has already guaranteed that if the agricultural bill is the measure brought back at three o'clock today when the House next deals with legislation, we will help make sure that that legislation passes. On legislation, we are willing to negotiate; we are willing to guarantee.

Mr. Speaker, on March 19, Kimberly-Clark outlined its position on the sale of the Spruce Falls Pulp and Paper Company in Kapuskasing.
Kimberly-Clark has set a purchase deadline of April 30, 1991. This deadline creates unwarranted pressure on the purchasing employee group by withdrawing its exclusive buying rights. The deadline also applies to the sale of the Smokey Falls dam to the Ontario government. This time restriction will not permit a complete environmental assessment.
In 1983 Kimberly-Clark decided not to modernize Spruce Falls. This was inappropriate. As a corporate citizen it has failed miserably to honour its commitment to the workers.
The Government of Ontario could retaliate by avoiding the forest management agreement which would leave Spruce Falls without a wood supply for next year. A new FMA would be renegotiated with a new owner.
Kimberly-Clark is shifting its corporate responsibility to the province. Suddenly, it has forgotten the profits it has made in the past 63 years. Kimberly-Clark has the
March 26, 1991

moral responsibility to secure work for the 1,200 workers it plans to lay off.

Mr. Speaker, many Canadians are frustrated when Telemarketing calls intrude upon their personal lives.
Today I would like to congratulate the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and the Canadian Direct Marketing Association for establishing standards of conduct that respect consumer privacy.
I am especially pleased to see the leadership that the minister has demonstrated by making businesses responsible for maintaining acceptable standards that are in the consumer interest.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday afternoon the Standing Committee on Environment released its third report on global warming fittingly entitled Out of Balance: The Risks of Irreversible Climate Change. The report is based on hearings that extended over eight months, a review of over 120 written submissions, and the testimony of more than 100 qualified witnesses.
The recommendations of the report are solid, comprehensive and realistic. Based on four principal premises, the report concludes that global warming is proven and validated scientifically, that global warming is the inevitable consequence of past and present human activity, that global warming is a dire threat to Canada and the entire planet, and that the time to act is now, without delay.
In memory of Dean Clay, the committee's principal researcher and adviser who passed away suddenly on October 22, 1990, let me say that Dean's outstanding assistance and contribution on this pressing global issue will be a legacy for generations to come.

Mr. Speaker, potato farmers in Prince Edward Island are still waiting
for the federal government to come forward with its compensation package to assist those farmers affected by the PVY-N virus.
Farmers are looking to plant their crops within five weeks and must get their seed lined up. The uncertainty resulting from this delay is not only causing anxiety among the farmers. It is affecting their ability to obtain operating credit.
This problem does not only affect the potato industry. It has repercussions on the entire economy of my province.
Surely the welfare and security of the potato industry should be a priority. The U.S. ban was put in place almost two months ago. In that length of time surely this government has been able to put together the required compensation package.
I call on the federal government to delay no longer, to let the farmers of Prince Edward Island know where they stand, and to announce immediately a full and comprehensive compensation package.

Mr. Speaker, at the end of this week it will be two years since the last federal-provincial forestry agreement in Saskatchewan expired.
I have lost track of how many times this government has told me that an agreement is just around the comer. The Minister of Forestry himself came to Prince Albert last August and said it would be there by Christmas. Finally word circulated that on March 11a new agreement would finally be signed.
A new agreement was signed yesterday in Manitoba, but what has happened in Saskatchewan? On March 6, Grant Devine's election timetable was derailed by the boundaries fiasco and we have not seen hide nor hair of the agreement since.
This farce has gone on long enough.
The sustainable development of Saskatchewan's forests and the livelihood of the people living in those forests are simply too important to be held hostage by Grant Devine's election shenanigans.

March 26, 1991
Therefore I call on this government to stop playing footsie with Grant Devine on this issue and to start giving Saskatchewan's forests and the forest communities the support it has promised for so long.

Mr. Speaker, medicare is the cornerstone of the social system, cherished by all Canadians. However few understand the actual cost of these excellent services, for example that it is much more expensive to treat minor health problems at hospital emergency wards rather than in doctors' offices.
In this age of computers we should provide eveiyone with a print-out showing the real cost of medical services received each year. Then we would have an informed public able to make more cost effective use of medicare, with resulting savings for all taxpayers.
We already get print-outs showing our Canada Pension entitlement. I urge the federal government and the provinces to give Canadians personal information about the actual cost of their medicare.

Mr. Speaker, the recently announced $80 million joint expenditure by the province of Quebec and the federal government should be looked upon as a positive step by all levels of government.
The 75-25 sharing arrangement to develop municipal roads, sewage and water facilities for industrial projects will be welcomed, I am sure, by the municipalities that benefit from it.
With a similar need for funds for regional development by municipalities in all provinces, it is hoped that the minister responsible will advise the House soon what the criteria are for provinces to apply for this assistance or tell us when similar cost sharing programs will be announced for other provinces.
The government is finally seeing the folly in its deindustrialization process and has taken a step in the right direction with Quebec, a step which should be repeated with all other provinces.

vatives far behind on environmentally responsible energy policy.
As just one example, the Ontario government has ordered Ontario Hydro to divert $240 million, that is $60 million per year for four years, from nuclear energy development into reducing demand through energy conservation and efficiency.

Mr. Speaker, my constituents send me a very loud and clear message that in the next round of constitutional discussions native issues must be a major priority.
They do not want to see any more violence or armed confrontation. They do want to see a rapid and just settlement of all outstanding legitimate claims of native Canadians whether they involve land, self-government or sovereignty.
Mr. Speaker, you and I know that is not an easy task. Native leaders do not always agree with one another, let alone the government. The Mohawks at Oka, for example, are reportedly divided into seven factions all claiming to be the sole legitimate community leaders.
However it is essential that the government at least be seen to be doing all that it can to find a solution, and so far in spite of the minister's efforts that message is just not getting through.

I am proud to wear this badge which says that enlightened men respect and encourage women seeking equity. It was presented to me at the first exhibition of educational services for francophone women which took place in Orleans in the riding of Carleton-Gloucester.

Mr. Speaker, I was astounded yesterday to find that it has cost up to $8,000 each to research answers to questions on the Order

March 26, 1991
Paper. In fact, some shared questions involving more than one department could exceed that $8,000 figure.
None of us can question the fact that we have the right, indeed the responsibility, to be thorough, but we also have the obligation to set an example of fiscal responsibility.

A general consensus developed within this commission made up of various interests and groups, except for the Liberal Party Of Canada, the Progressive Conservative Party, and the Equality Party. Mr. Speaker, Quebec is serenely preparing for the future.
Within eighteen months Canada will have an opportunity to make formal offers to the people of Quebec. Ever more Quebecers are becoming aware that the referendum campaign has just begun and that, by October 26, 1992 at the latest, the majority of men and women in the province will vote in favour of the only realistic and practical option, sovereignty.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw the attention of the House to an article in today's edition of The Ottawa Citizen which describes the construction of Canada's pavilion at Expo 92 in Seville, Spain as being on time and on budget.
Mr. Gordon Smith, Canada's Deputy Commissioner General to Expo 92, is quoted as saying:
We're ahead because we're the best organized country here, we planned and made decisions early on.
I have in my possession an internal External Affairs document which paints a much different picture, a much costlier picture of the construction of the Canadian pavilion. Under the heading of immediate problem, the document says:
The situation today is that we are on time but not on budget, and we may need to return to TB for extra funding in the magnitude of $10 million.
In fact, the budget for the Canadian pavilion at Expo 92 has been revised upward by $2.4 billion in the 1990 Supplementary Estimates. This represents a 42 per cent increase in less than one year.
I hope the minister of external affairs will see fit to correct the misleading impression this story leaves in The Ottawa Citizen of the true cost of the Canadian pavilion and let Canadians know just how much of a financial bath we can expect to take.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
In the wee hours of the morning today a vote was taken at the Belanger-Campeau Commission in Quebec which could set the stage for the end of Canada.
At a time when leadership means standing to be counted, the Prime Minister and his party abstained in the vote.
Why did the Prime Minister refuse to stand and be counted for Canada?

Mr. Speaker, as usual my friend, the Acting Leader of the Opposition is, to put it charitably, only partly right.
In the wee hours of this morning there was not one vote. There were many votes taken at the Belanger-Campeau Commission, including the key vote which asked the members to endorse sovereignty as the preferred choice of Quebecers. The member of this government, Mr. Hogue, along with a member of her party, voted solidly against that petition.

Their bargaining position?

Their bargaining position, exactly. It is one that would be set out by the Government of the Province of Quebec.

I find it very interesting that last week the Acting Leader of the Opposition rose and asked all parties in the House to depoliticize the question of national unity and today, quite in error and with mischief, is trying to politicize something that should be depoliticized.

Given the tight schedule we are stuck with, whether we like it or not, when will the Prime Minister show national leadership and disclose his own agenda so that a consensus can be achieved as to the necessary reforms for a new Canada?

Indeed, Mr. Speaker, my friend is absolutely right. The status quo is no longer satisfactory and has not been since the Constitution was patriated in 1981-1982. In-depth changes were needed and some, although modest, were agreed upon in the Meech Lake Accord which my friend supported.
In spite of these modest changes endorsed by the Liberal Party as well as the New Democratic Party, a Premier, the Premier of Newfoundland, failed to have them confirmed by a vote in the legislature of his province.
The fact remains nonetheless that deep changes are needed as I advocated in a speech I made in Buckingham. As a matter of fact, that is one of the reasons for setting up the Spicer Commission as well as the Ed-wards-Beaudoin Special Joint Committee. It is also one of the reasons why the government House leader gave notice to the hon. members last week that they will be involved more closely in a parliamentary process aimed precisely at preparing reforms for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister is accusing me of politicizing the debate. I say that if anyone in this House is politicizing the debate, that person, is right across the way. When the time comes to make a critical decision on a question as

fundamental as the unity of Canada, people understand yes, they understand no, but they don't understand abstention.
Hear, hear!

Oh, oh.

speechtext: I think we will have to move along. The hon. member for LaSalle-Emard.

Hear, hear.

industrial policy, no hope. The true crisis in Confederation is that this nation-

Mr. Speaker, Canada was not founded by a Parliamentary committee. It was built by men and women who wanted a better future for themselves and their children. It is not a Parliamentary committee which will decide today whether our children will be entitled to the same privileges as Canadian citizens. The purpose of the Meech Lake Accord was to bring Quebec back into the Canadian constitutional fold. Its failure will not prevent us as Parliamentarians and Canadians eager to preserve the integrity and the unity of our great country to make the necessary effort in order to ensure the participation

of Parliamentarians who will give a new direction to a strong and united Canada.

A supplementary, Mr. Speaker. I agree that of course parliamentarians are very important in this debate. However, the Constitution of a country is not between parliamentarians, it is not between governments, but it is between a nation and its people.
I want to say to the Prime Minister that we cannot be put in the position of last year, where we had a crisis kind of week and there is not now an elected federal leader in this country, including myself, which has the mandate to fundamentally restructure the country.
I say to the Prime Minister that the kind of work that has to be done will require the support, not just of parliamentarians, not just of provincial and territorial leaders, but of the people of Canada.
How does the Prime Minister propose to get that support and that mandate from the Canadian people for a new Constitution and Canadian unity?

Mr. Speaker, is my hon. friend putting in doubt the traditions of the British parliamentary system whereby a government seeks a mandate and is elected for a given period of time? The NDP says it is archaic. Go tell Bob Rae it is archaic. He says he has a mandate that lasts five years and he plans to exercise it. That is what I am going to do.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister knows, Canadians know, that this government has no mandate from the Canadian people to fundamentally restructure this country.
It is essential, if we are not going to go through the high stakes, high pressure tactics used last summer, and be thrust into next summer before a referendum in Quebec, through some kind of Russian roulette crisis tactic again, that this Prime Minister and this government seek a mandate from the Canadian people for a vision of Canadian unity and a Canada that can go into the 21st century.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. I am really disappointed by these paragons of procedural virtue to my left who try to pretend one thing and practise another.
Hear, hear.
